rule: Method: `Type#member`. Nested types are dotted: `Outer.Inner#m`. Some languages prefix a module/package qualifier with dots (see per-language notes). `self.m()` / `this.m()` / a bare call to a member of the enclosing type → `Type#m`. If `m` is defined only on a superclass that is in the scan, the callee is `Superclass#m`. **Java / Kotlin / C# / Groovy / Scala**: package/namespace-qualified: `com.x.C#m`; an external type is qualified through its explicit import. Kotlin top-level functions `com.x.f`. A Groovy script (a file with top-level code or functions) is a class named after the file: its functions are `pkg.Script#f`, its top-level code `pkg.Script#run`. Generic/template type arguments are dropped from every ID (`HashSet#<init>`). Overloads share one ID. Companion-object members flatten onto the class.
notes: Companion object Shop's members flatten onto class Shop (SPEC: 'Companion-object members flatten onto the class'), so Shop.base() is app.Shop#base and the class Clerk nested in the companion is app.Shop.Clerk. inner is bound by `= new Shop.Clerk()` (decision A) so inner.serve() is app.Shop.Clerk#serve, high. A standalone object (Pricing) is the type Pricing. Local vals inside method bodies are not field initializers. call_type convention used throughout: a call on a receiver (written, or the implicit this/object of a bare member call) is `method`; a call of a named nested function or an unresolved bare name is `direct`; `new`/super/this constructor calls are `constructor`; calls through function values are `callback`. SPEC lists the call_type values but does not define direct vs method beyond this.
